items.question: What do you see as the unresolved challenge in using machine learning to bring together the many kinds of data collected from cancer patients?
items.object: Statistical power and integrating cancer patient data in machine learning
items.answer: So a lot of this comes down to statistics and statistical power still, right? We generate a ton of data. So if we think about cancer patients—and I think a lot about cancer patients—cancer from a machine learning perspective is really interesting because the patients go to the doctor a lot because they're undergoing treatment. They're getting imaged every four to six weeks. So we're getting a lot of data on them. They're having a tumor removed, and then we're sending that tumor for sequencing. We're sending that tumor to be sliced up and put on a pathology slide and looked at. That's another image. So we're generating a lot of data in those patients, and how we put that data together is still a big question that I think we need to solve. Some of it is again related to statistical power, right? There's still—you know, if you're extracting a lot of variables from a lot of images, from a lot of clinical data points, and you don't have that many patients, you still are running into an overfitting problem. You're still sort of doing this torturing of data, and I joke with my clinical collaborators that I can predict anything from anything if you give me a small enough number of patients and enough data points. So those are still problems that we have, and AI tools don't magically get you past those problems of basic statistics, right? So I think that's still a very open area.

items.question: How do you understand statistical nomograms as a form of precision medicine?
items.object: Statistical nomograms as precision medicine
items.answer: There's some really simple methods of precision medicine, and we call those statistical nomograms. And these are really fascinating devices that researchers, statisticians, clinicians come up with for making very simple decisions based on multiple variables. If you look at these things, they're sheets of paper that have rulers on them, and you go through each of the steps. So the first ruler might be, is this person male or female? Oh, they're male. Okay. So let's say this is prostate cancer, right? So then it might come to another variable, and then we say, okay, is it over this amount or under this amount? And then we move over to this part of the nomogram. And as you get down to the bottom of this map, there's a decision at the bottom. If you're over to this side, then you're positive for prostate cancer. If you're over to the other side, then maybe you're negative or you're low risk of prostate cancer. And so that's existed for a really long time. And that's honestly a version of machine learning, right? It's a multivariable model. And this is just a very simple way to produce those models for clinicians to understand and honestly for patients to understand too.

items.answer: We certainly have models looking at genetic data. So we take your tumor. For example, in the cancer case, we take a piece of that tumor and we subject it to tests. items.answer: So, from my perspective, again, we have a patient, we give them the most common treatment, but they might not actually fit that most common treatment. items.question: How do you understand the rationale for giving chemotherapy or immunotherapy before removing a visible cancerous tumor?
items.object: Giving chemotherapy or immunotherapy before removing a visible tumor
items.answer: There's cancer that you see, but there's cancer that you don't see, right? And just because we can see it, you may have additional cancer that we're not seeing yet. You may have tumor cells that are going through your body. And so the idea is if we give you a medication, a chemotherapy or an immunotherapy up front, then maybe we would destroy all of those cancer cells in your body, and then you wouldn't continue to have a recurrence of that cancer or that cancer coming back. And so that's a really new thought. It was always—we always thought for decades that a tumor was a tumor and that was the thing you wanted to get rid of. But now we understand that you can have cancer that we're not quite seeing yet. You can have tumor cells that are going all through your body, and those are the ones that we also want to kill.

If you're walking a little funny. When I was in New York, we had something called the get up and go test. If you could get up out of bed and go, then you could be eligible for surgery. That's not information that we collect, right? But it's information that we know: if a patient is well enough to get up and go, they're well enough that they can undergo an aggressive surgery.

items.question: How do you understand an experienced radiologist’s ability to see a cancer that other people have missed?
items.object: Experienced radiologists’ ability to detect cancers that others miss
items.answer: I have a friend and former colleague that's a radiologist, and he can see things that other people don't see. And it's because he's looked at so many images for so long. When I was at the cancer center, one of the things that we do is have what's called tumor board meetings. These are for specific cancers. We were in the liver and pancreas cancer tumor board meeting. So this is radiologists, oncologists, surgeons, everybody that could see these patients. The radiologist sits at the front and they put up images and then they discuss the images and everybody asks questions. The radiologist puts up the image of the liver and we're all looking at it, and everyone's getting cranky because there's no tumor in the liver. Why are we looking at this patient? We need to get on with our lives. And he starts playing with it and he says, "No, everyone be quiet." He just stops listening and he starts playing with the image and playing with how the contrast is working. And all of a sudden you see this 8 cm liver cancer just kind of appear out of the background, right? Could we have seen that with AI? Maybe. Maybe if we trained it right. But that was magical to me that this was a patient that had been passed around to a number of different institutions with all of these symptoms that pointed to liver cancer, but nobody could see a liver cancer, and then this guy sees it.

items.question: How has your thinking changed about whether patient databanks such as UK Biobank and NIH All of Us contain enough information to study rare diseases?
items.object: Patient databanks such as UK Biobank and NIH All of Us
items.answer: Something that's happened over the last decade is that we've invested in the idea of generating a lot of data on patients, whether or not those patients have disease. So we have the UK Biobank as a great example of this, where we've prospectively enrolled patients, we've consented them, and then we collect all kinds of data on those patients: longitudinal imaging, genomic studies, all different types of studies. These patients at the time of enrollment may not have had a disease, but as we study them over 10 years and we keep collecting information on them, they start to develop cancer, they start to develop heart disease, and then we can start looking at different signals within those populations. In the US we have something called All of Us, NIH All of Us, where they're doing something similar and collecting this data. We always thought that there wouldn't be enough data, that there wouldn't be enough variation in the data. If you're looking at pancreas cancer, for example, it's still an extremely rare disease. So you would need tens of millions of healthy patients to follow who's going to get a pancreas cancer. So that's what we always thought. Well, this doesn't seem to be the case. It seems to be the case that we actually have enough information in these databanks to do some of this analysis.

items.question: How do you see Mendelian randomization enabling the study of “human knockouts” using large human databanks?
items.object: Mendelian randomization and the idea of a human knockout
items.answer: So we've got animals that are with drugs that are developed based on them that aren't replicating. We have these huge databanks. In the 2020s this idea of Mendelian randomization came up, and the idea of Mendelian randomization is that within the population of humans there are genes that are turned off and on naturally, just by randomization. And so this is the idea that we developed of a human knockout. This idea that if you had enough humans and their data to study, you could have genes turned on and off, and then you could study naturally.

items.question: How do you assess the potential of UK Biobank data for studying human knockouts through naturally occurring genetic variation?
items.object: Using UK Biobank data to study human knockouts through naturally occurring genetic variation
items.answer: What we showed is that you can do analysis of UK Biobank data and you can show that this natural randomization of turning these genes on and off gives you enough variability that you can then test—in our case we looked at cardiovascular outcomes. The reason we did that is because cardiovascular outcomes are very common. That means that within these 500,000 patients, there's enough of this natural variation in the genes, and then there's enough outcomes in cardiovascular diseases that we can actually start making these human knockouts. And so we actually showed that you could replicate, I think it was 27 cardiovascular trials of these different genes turned on and off and targets made for these genes in UK Biobank data. We were shocked that it worked. We really didn't think it was going to work, but it worked really well. And now we've done this across many different targets, these genes that are turned on and off. And then the idea would be as the UK Biobank data gets more mature, these patients start to have other things wrong with them like cancer, like other diseases, that you could actually study these human knockouts. And that's our idea. And it's actually working, and we're the most surprised that it's working of everyone.

items.question: What do you see as the motivation for replacing animals with computational models in drug development?

items.answer: So the National Institutes of Health in the US wants to see these types of computational models used instead of animals. For me, epidemiology and biostatistics is still super important. If you're doing AI on some cohort that doesn't make sense, garbage in is garbage out, right? items.question: How do you see AI changing healthcare over the next ten years?
items.object: AI’s role in healthcare over the next ten years
items.answer: I think what we're going to see is an acceptance of AI, at least from a health care perspective, because I think there's real ways that we can make improvements for actual people using artificial intelligence tools, probably ones that already exist. We probably honestly don't even need new ones that make a difference for patients, right? And I think that would be a huge win for AI. It would be a huge win for medicine. It would be a huge win for patients. And so I think we're going to see that. It's going to be tools that are simple. It's going to be tools that are complex. And I think that's really exciting. LLMs really brought AI to the clinic, for better or for worse, right? So you're getting experience now with AI in the regular world. And so I think certainly in medicine, we have the opportunity to be the good guys, right? And to be the ones that do it right and to be the ones that do it while mitigating bias and considering AI safety and all of these very important things. And I think in 10 years we'll be at a position where we've actually changed outcomes for patients and changed the world, really.
